title: Chapter 15 — Ventilation
intro: The most under-sold category — CFM pairing, duct reality, hood types, and the system sale.

sections.title: The Most Under-Sold Category
content: Ventilation is the most under-sold category on the floor. Most salespeople treat it as an afterthought — 'Do you need a hood?' after the range is sold. This is backwards. Proper ventilation is required by code in many jurisdictions, affects indoor air quality, and represents $500–$4,000 in additional ticket value. Sell the hood WITH the cooking product, not after.

**Why ventilation matters.** Gas cooking produces combustion byproducts (carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide). All cooking produces grease particles, moisture, and odors. Without adequate ventilation, these accumulate — grease coats cabinets, moisture feeds mold, odors linger. In a sealed modern home with energy-efficient windows, cooking exhaust has nowhere to go without mechanical ventilation.

sections.title: Hood Types
content: **Wall-Mount Chimney Hood.** Mounts on the wall above a range against the wall. The most common and most effective configuration. Available in 30" and 36" standard widths. Stainless steel, glass canopy, or decorative designs. CFM ratings from 300 to 1,200+.

**Island Hood.** Suspended from the ceiling above an island cooktop or range. Requires ducting through the ceiling. More CFM required than wall-mount because there's no wall to help contain the capture area. Typically 600–1,200 CFM. Premium product — $1,500–$5,000+.

**Under-Cabinet Hood.** Mounts under a wall cabinet directly above the range. Compact, affordable, effective for standard installations. 30" standard. $150–$800. Most budget and mid-range kitchens use under-cabinet hoods.

**Insert/Liner.** The ventilation mechanism installs inside a custom wood or plaster hood surround. The customer gets a custom kitchen look with professional ventilation performance. Popular in luxury and custom kitchens. Brands: Vent-A-Hood, Best, Zephyr, Broan.

**Over-the-Range Microwave (OTR).** Combines a microwave with basic ventilation. 300–400 CFM typical. The most common ventilation 'solution' in North America — but the weakest performer. Adequate for light cooking; inadequate for serious cooking or gas ranges over 40,000 BTU. The trade-up from an OTR to a proper hood is a great upsell.

**Downdraft.** Rises from behind or beside the cooktop, or pulls air downward through the cooking surface. For islands and peninsulas where overhead ventilation is impossible. Less effective than overhead hoods because hot air rises (you're fighting physics). GE Profile, JennAir, KitchenAid, Best. Last resort, not first choice.

sections.title: CFM: The Number That Matters
content: CFM = Cubic Feet per Minute of air the hood can move. More CFM = more ventilation capacity.
**Rule of thumb for gas:** 1 CFM per 100 BTU of cooking output. A 60,000 BTU rangetop needs a 600 CFM hood minimum.
**Rule of thumb for electric/induction:** 10x the cooktop width in inches. A 36" induction cooktop needs ~360 CFM.

**Make-up air.** In many jurisdictions, hoods over 300–400 CFM require make-up air — a system that brings fresh air in to replace the air being exhausted. Without it, the hood creates negative pressure that can backdraft gas appliances (dangerous), pull conditioned air out of the house, and cause doors to slam. This is a code requirement the customer needs to know about BEFORE they fall in love with a 1,200 CFM hood. Installation cost for make-up air: $1,000–$3,000+.

**Noise.** Hood noise is measured in sones. 1 sone = quiet refrigerator. 4 sones = normal conversation level. 8+ sones = loud. Most hoods are loudest at max speed. Premium hoods offer variable speed with lower noise at cooking speeds and max CFM for boiling and searing.

sections.title: Duct vs Ductless
content: **Ducted (vented).** Air is exhausted outside through ductwork. Far more effective. Always the preferred choice when ductwork is possible. Duct size matters — most hoods want 6" or 8" round duct. Longer duct runs and elbows reduce effective CFM.

**Ductless (recirculating).** Air passes through charcoal filters and recirculates back into the kitchen. Removes some odor and grease but does NOT remove moisture, heat, or combustion gases. Use only when ducting is truly impossible. Charcoal filters need replacement every 3–6 months — recurring cost for the customer.

**Always recommend ducted.** If the customer says 'I can't vent to the outside,' ask where the range is positioned and whether there's a path through the wall, ceiling, or soffit. Many 'impossible' vent installations just need a creative duct path.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
content: Never sell a range without discussing ventilation. Ask: 'What's above your cooking surface right now?' If they say an OTR microwave or nothing, you have a ventilation sale. Match the hood to the cooking product — a $10,000 Wolf range with a $200 recirculating hood is a mismatch that makes you look uninformed. Know your local code on make-up air thresholds.
